turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Doctor, sorry, I know I'm early, but my back's been crook and I can't stop thinking it's something bad.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're alright, sit down. Start wherever you like.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Low back, across the belt line. A few weeks, or since the move, I honestly can't tell which.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): When was the move?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Six weeks last Saturday... no, three weeks last Saturday. I keep mixing it up. Whether the pain started before that or on the weekend we lifted everything, I don't know.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the start date fuzzy then. Describe the pain.
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Deep ache. Bending to pick up a box, or a cough, it grabs. I was going to say six out of ten, no, seven. Lying flat on the floor eases it.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): So bending and a cough set it off, and lying down helps. Desk job, or on the tools?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Warehouse, pick and pack. Boxes all day. By the arvo I'm stuffed and ratty.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any numbness or pins and needles down either leg?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): It doesn't shoot down the leg either, it just stays in the back. There was this thing in the ute where I—
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Sorry, go on, the ute?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): I sat on my foot and it went to sleep, all tingly, but that was the foot, not a nerve from the back. Numbness down the leg? No. I don't have that.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Good, that's clear. Any trouble passing urine, leaking, or a numb feeling in the saddle area?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Saddle? Like horse riding? I don't...
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Between the legs, the parts that sit on a saddle. And the bladder.
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Oh. No. Weeing's normal, and no numbness there. I thought you meant actual horse riding for a second, sorry.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): No worries. Any fever, sweats, feeling shivery?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No temps at all. I feel well, which almost makes me more worried, like it's hiding.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): And weight loss, without trying?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): The kitchen's still in boxes so I've been skipping lunch, and the pants are looser. I haven't weighed myself, so it could be a kilo or just the belt. I don't know.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Okay, I won't call that definite weight loss. What painkillers are you on?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Panadol. I was taking two grams... no, that's wrong, one gram, twice a day. Two of the five hundred milligram tablets, morning and night.
[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): The chemist download on your file has ibuprofen six hundred milligrams three times a day as well.
[SEG0025] person_1 (PATIENT): Nah, that's not me. I take the four hundred milligram Nurofen, twice a day, with food if I remember. Three times would wreck me. Must be a stuffed-up download.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hmm. Two different doses and two different frequencies, and the box isn't here, so I can't pick a winner. Did you bring it?
[SEG0027] person_1 (PATIENT): Left it in the ute. Is six hundred even safe? I googled stomach bleeds at two am.

[SEG0028] person_2 (DOCTOR): Six hundred is a real prescription dose, but if you're swallowing four hundreds, you're not on six hundred. Short courses with food are usually fine. Any black bowel motions, or heartburn?
[SEG0029] person_1 (PATIENT): No black stools. A bit of heartburn if I take them before breakfast, nothing dramatic. My uncle had a bleed and now I spiral.
[SEG0030] person_2 (DOCTOR): Understood. I won't ignore the heartburn. Allergies to any medicines?
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Nothing. Penicillin was fine when I had tonsillitis years back.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any back surgery, cancer, long-term steroids, or thin bones?

[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No surgery, ever, and no cancer. I don't take steroids, and my bones are fine as far as I know. Dad's back was crook from years on the farm, not a proper disease. Is farm back hereditary, or is that a stupid question?
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not a stupid question. Heavy work runs in families more than a gene does, usually. Anyone with inflammatory arthritis, or ankylosing spondylitis?
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Mum's got arthritis in her hands, the knobbly kind. I don't know the spondylitis thing. Nobody's been in a wheelchair. Am I going to be?
[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm not seeing a wheelchair in this story. We'll come to why. Do you smoke?
[SEG0037] person_1 (PATIENT): Never. Not even at school. And before you ask, a couple of beers Saturday arvo, that's it. Does alcohol make backs worse? I can stop.
[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Weekend beers at that level aren't the driver here. You don't need to quit for this. How's your sleep been?
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): Rubbish. I roll over and it wakes me, three or four times, and then I lie there picturing a disc and a surgeon. Is it a slipped disc?
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me look before I answer that. Shirt up, stand for me. I'm watching how you move.
[SEG0041] person_1 (PATIENT): It pulls when I come up from bending. Is that the disc?

[SEG0042] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're standing a bit flexed. Forward bend, your fingertips reach about the knees, and that's where it grabs. You can extend, but it's sore. The spine midline isn't tender. The muscle either side is.
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise is comfortable both sides. Strength, reflexes, and the pulses in the feet are all normal. No nerve stretch.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): So nothing's trapped? Because when I cough it twinges, and I read that's a disc.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): A cough can tug a sore bit of back without a trapped nerve. With that leg exam, I'm not thinking of a pinched nerve today. Is the pain worst first thing in the morning, easing as you walk about?
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): Opposite. Mornings are the best part. It's after the shift, the lifting, that I'm ruined.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): That pattern is mechanical strain. I was going to send you for a lumbar X-ray this week, because—
[SEG0048] person_1 (PATIENT): It's broken, isn't it. Do I need a CT? An MRI?

[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me finish. It isn't the story of a break. No fever, no cancer history, no numbness, bladder's fine, so actually I do not want an X-ray this week. Early films mostly show ordinary changes and frighten people.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): You're backing off the scan? What if it's a tumour and the pants thing was the clue?

[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'm changing the plan because the normal exam and the lack of red flags make a tumour very unlikely. A real unexplained weight drop, pain at night that won't settle, or fever would push me to image. You haven't described those.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): Should I buy scales? I will if you say. I just need someone to tell me what to do. Work won't wait, the rent and the move wiped the savings.

[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Optional, jot a weight if you already have scales, don't go buying a project. For work, light duties, no repetitive lifting over ten kilos for a fortnight. Keep walking. Bed rest will make it worse.
[SEG0054] person_1 (PATIENT): Ten kilos. Our totes are fifteen, easy. I'll ask the supervisor. Are you going to prescribe something stronger, like naproxen? A bloke at work takes that.

[SEG0055] person_2 (DOCTOR): I nearly did, naproxen five hundred milligrams twice a day was on the tip of my pen. Then I remembered you're already on an anti-inflammatory and we can't even agree the dose. Stacking naproxen on ibuprofen is how people get the bleed your uncle had, so no, I am not prescribing it.
[SEG0056] person_1 (PATIENT): So I'm stuck with Panadol? That's it?

[SEG0057] person_2 (DOCTOR): Paracetamol one gram twice a day, the way you corrected it to, is the regular one. Keep the ibuprofen with food, and don't climb above whatever the four hundred packet allows, until we sight the box. Heartburn again, you stop the ibuprofen.
[SEG0058] person_1 (PATIENT): And ignore the six hundred on the file?
[SEG0059] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Ignore six hundred three times a day until the box or a photo says otherwise. Bring it next visit. I can't resolve that number today.
[SEG0060] person_1 (PATIENT): What about physio? My mate reckons one session and he was sweet.

[SEG0061] person_2 (DOCTOR): I was going to refer you to physio today. Public wait is months, and you've just said the move cleaned out your savings, so a private physio isn't fair to spring on you. I'll print an exercise sheet instead.
[SEG0062] person_1 (PATIENT): When do I come back? And if I'm not better, then physio?

[SEG0063] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks regardless, so I can recheck the legs and look at that box. If you're not clearly better then, I'll refer you to physio and we'll organise the lumbar X-ray at that point. Not before.
[SEG0064] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. What if before that I can't wee, or the legs go numb, or I get a fever with it?
[SEG0065] person_2 (DOCTOR): Emergency department the same day. Don't wait for the appointment. Those, or new weakness, are the reasons to go in.
[SEG0066] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I have something on paper for the boss? He won't do light duties on my say-so.
[SEG0067] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll write a light-duties certificate for two weeks, lifting limit ten kilograms. Collect it from the desk on the way out.
[SEG0068] person_1 (PATIENT): The exercises. Are they going to make it worse? I don't want to snap something.
[SEG0069] person_2 (DOCTOR): Gentle only. Pelvic tilts, short walks, a heat pack on those side muscles. Stop if pain starts shooting down a leg. No bed rest, no hero stretches.
[SEG0070] person_1 (PATIENT): And Panadol, morning and night, one gram. What if the middle of the day is awful? Can I take more, or is that when people wreck their liver?

[SEG0071] person_2 (DOCTOR): You can space one gram up to four times in a day, and you must not go over four grams in twenty-four hours. Twice a day, as you're doing, is fine. No extra products from the chemist on top.
[SEG0072] person_1 (PATIENT): Four grams is the ceiling. My cousin lives on codeine for his back. Should I get some?
[SEG0073] person_2 (DOCTOR): No codeine. It bungs you up and it isn't better than paracetamol and movement for this. I'm not prescribing it.
[SEG0074] person_1 (PATIENT): Is there a chance this is ankyl-whatever, the thing you said, because Mum's hands are bad?

[SEG0075] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hand osteoarthritis in your mum doesn't give you ankylosing spondylitis. Your pain's worse after work, not the early-morning inflammatory pattern. I don't think that's what this is.
[SEG0076] person_1 (PATIENT): So your actual opinion, in normal words?
[SEG0077] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mechanical low back pain from lifting. Provisional, not a scan-proven label. The exam doesn't show a trapped nerve. That's the working impression.
[SEG0078] person_1 (PATIENT): And I can still work if they drop the heavy totes?
[SEG0079] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes. Light duties, walking, the tablets we just set. If the supervisor pushes back, the certificate says ten kilograms.
[SEG0080] person_1 (PATIENT): I might still google. I know you'll tell me not to.
[SEG0081] person_2 (DOCTOR): If you google, stick to red flags, not tumour lists. Bring the ibuprofen box or a photo, do the sheet, and I'll see you in two weeks even if you're heaps better.
[SEG0082] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Thanks for not rushing me out. I'll try to leave the wheelchair idea in the car park.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Mother's hand arthritis/osteoarthritis supported, but it was reported by patient, not doctor.
Move timing supported as three weeks ago, but living status=current is not stated.
bad.text: living (description=Moved house three weeks ago, status=current, reported_by=patient)

omissions.text: Ibuprofen dose/frequency actually reported by the patient was 400 mg twice a day with food if remembered; this is missing from the medication entry, which lists ibuprofen without dose or frequency.
The patient denied sweats and feeling shivery in addition to denying fever/temps.
Bowel leakage/incontinence was asked about ('leaking') and denied as part of bladder/bowel red flags, but only bladder dysfunction is recorded.
The patient denied any medicine allergies and specifically said penicillin had been tolerated previously when treated for tonsillitis years ago.
Sleep disturbance detail is incomplete: the patient said sleep was 'rubbish', rolling over wakes them, and they wake three or four times then lie awake worrying.
Doctor documented normal lower-limb strength, reflexes, and foot pulses, and also stated there was 'no nerve stretch'; the absence of a nerve stretch sign is not explicitly recorded.
The patient denied thin bones/osteoporosis ('my bones are fine as far as I know'), which was asked in screening for red flags but not recorded.
Family history included that no one was known to have ankylosing spondylitis/inflammatory arthritis; only mother's hand osteoarthritis and father's back pain were recorded.

The doctor explicitly advised no imaging now and explained that an early lumbar X-ray is not wanted this week because the exam was normal and there were no red flags; only the later conditional X-ray plan is recorded.

The doctor considered but decided against prescribing naproxen 500 mg twice a day because the patient was already taking an NSAID and the ibuprofen dose was unresolved; this medication decision is not recorded.
The doctor explicitly instructed the patient to ignore the erroneous ibuprofen 600 mg three-times-daily dose on the file until the box/photo confirms otherwise.

Physiotherapy was initially considered for immediate referral but deferred because public wait times are long and private physiotherapy was not affordable after the move; only the conditional future referral is recorded.
The patient can continue working on light duties if heavy lifting is avoided; this work advice/clearance was stated explicitly in addition to the certificate plan.
